endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: (b) Supplier has disclosed to Customer, all artificial intelligence technology it has embedded in or provided with the Cloud Services, Software, Products and/or Services;

endorsements.title: Considerations for the regulation of generative AI-enabled medical devices (discussion paper)
endorsements.quote: Whether the device recognizes safety-critical clinical states and initiates escalation that is timely, clear, actionable, and appropriately empathetic. Both under-escalation (failing to escalate when clinically necessary) and over-escalation (escalating when not clinically indicated) are relevant failures.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology
endorsements.quote: Include relevant AI Actors in the GAI system risk identification process.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether vendor disclosure of foundation models, third-party components, agent capabilities, and a software bill of materials at intake reduces unassessed failures or outages, and no study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation currently rests on three governance and regulatory documents, only one of which directly calls for disclosure of embedded AI technology.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The endorsements are expert consensus documents, which GRADE treats as opinion rather than evidence of effect. The claim that disclosure prevents failure modes or outages remains an untested hypothesis.

The CHAI playbook lists disclosure of all embedded AI technology as a must-level contract term, but it does not name a software bill of materials. The NIST Generative AI Profile asks that relevant AI actors join risk identification, which may imply upstream disclosure. The FDA discussion paper addresses escalation behavior and bears only indirectly on supply-chain transparency.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems or procurements with and without structured upstream disclosure and software bills of materials at intake, measuring outcomes such as the number of dependency-related incidents, time to identify an affected product when an upstream model changes or fails, unplanned downtime, and the staff time required to review disclosures. Even descriptive studies documenting how often hidden upstream models cause clinical AI failures would establish the size of the hazard.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested this practice in any population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy settings. Safety-net systems often have fewer staff to review vendor disclosures, and whether a disclosure requirement yields any benefit for them, or adds review burden without matching capacity, is unknown.
